newsitem.title: ITALY: Iran says one EU country blocked Rushdie deal.
newsitem.headline: Iran says one EU country blocked Rushdie deal.

text.p: Iran has twice come close to a deal to resolve the Salman Rushdie affair but a settlement was blocked each time by a single European Union country, Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati was quoted on Thursday as saying.

Velayati told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera that Iran had kept copies of the drafts of both accords, which he said had been negotiated under the Spanish and Italian EU presidencies from mid-1995 to mid-1996.
The newspaper said Velayati had hinted strongly that Britain had blocked a deal. "It's easy to guess who," the newspaper quoted him as saying.

Iran's late spiritual leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomenei issued a death edict or fatwa against British author Rushdie in 1989 because of alleged blasphemy against Islam in Rushdie's novel The Satanic Verses.
Rushdie was forced into hiding and the EU began what it calls a "critical dialogue" with Iran to get the fatwa lifted.
"We were twice on the verge of resolving the Rushdie affair, under the Spanish presidency in the second half of 1995 and under the Italian presidency last year," Velayati said.
"Fourteen of the 15 EU countries had reached an agreement with us. In both cases it was the 15th country that blocked everything at the last moment," he said.

A Foreign Office spokesman in London said Britain was working closely with its EU partners to get the fatwa removed and it would maintain pressure on Iran for "written assurances of safety" for Rushdie.
"We demand the lifting of the fatwa and nothing short of this will do," the spokesman said. "The reason there has been no deal is because Iran has not agreed to this."
Discussions with Iran were continuing, he said, and Britain continued to believe Rushdie was at serious risk.

Iran has said the edict against Rushdie is irrevocable although Velayati, who left Italy on Wednesday after two days of talks with the government, repeated the official line that Iran would not send anyone to kill the author.
"That is our line, our policy on the Rushdie case. But as you see there are still people who have interests in not resolving this problem," Velayati said.
Asked who, he said the United States and Britain had lost influence in Iran following the country's Islamic revolution.
"People who have lost space and power aren't able to tolerate it," he said.
The U.S. wants its European allies to cut off all links with Iran, which it regards as a sponsor of terrorism.
